articles.body:
Le grandi chiazze scure nello stretto di Hormuz si vedono anche dallo spazio. Per tutto il mese di ottobre le petroliere sono state colpite da missili o mine navali nello stretto, causando lo sversamento di greggio in mare. L’inquinamento si è esteso a tutto il golfo Persico, contaminando le coste e minacciando danni permanenti agli ecosistemi marini, che ospitano delfini, tartarughe e moltissime specie di pesci.

A otto mesi dall’inizio della guerra tra Stati Uniti e Iran, una delle rotte del petrolio più trafficate al mondo è al centro di un disastro ambientale in continua espansione.

Il blocco navale in vigore nello stretto ha reso quasi impossibile documentare l’inquinamento sul posto. Tuttavia, l’analisi delle immagini satellitari, unita alle testimonianze di esperti ambientali e biologi marini, aiuta a fare un quadro della situazione.

Lo stretto di Hormuz, l’unico passaggio marittimo tra il golfo Persico e il mar Arabico, ospita ecosistemi marini rigogliosi ma fragili, che comprendono barriere coralline, foreste di mangrovie e praterie marine che sostengono una ricca fauna marina.

Ha un ruolo vitale nella circolazione dell’acqua e delle sostanze nutritive, ed è sulla rotta migratoria dei mammiferi marini. Anche in tempo di pace i suoi ecosistemi avevano affrontato una pressione crescente dovuta al traffico marittimo, all’estrazione petrolifera e allo sviluppo costiero.

Il petrolio ricopre le piume degli uccelli, rendendogli difficile restare a galla e procurarsi da mangiare. Ricopre le radici delle mangrovie, impedendogli di assorbire ossigeno col rischio di causarne la morte.

Bernhard Riegl, biologo marino presso la Nova southeastern university in Florida, che studia il Golfo da più di trent’anni, avverte che il conflitto in corso potrebbe causare danni duraturi alle sue acque chiuse, già sottoposte a forti pressioni a causa della crisi climatica.

“Dato che il Golfo è poco profondo e l’estate è il periodo meno ventoso dell’anno, il calore atmosferico si trasforma rapidamente in calore oceanico, che uccide coralli, alghe e pesci. Non ci sono acque fredde e profonde che possano mescolarsi”, spiega Riegl.

“Tutti sanno che la presenza di petrolio nell’acqua non è una buona cosa. Ma nel contesto attuale le conseguenze potrebbero essere devastanti. Non esiste una ‘guerra pulita’, né per gli sfortunati esseri umani che si trovano coinvolti né per lo sfortunato ambiente naturale in cui si svolge il conflitto”.

Da quando è cominciata la guerra, il 28 febbraio, Greenpeace ha individuato più di cinquecento perdite di petrolio grazie al monitoraggio satellitare del golfo Persico, dello stretto di Hormuz e del mar Arabico. I risultati comprendono sversamenti significativi legati ad attacchi documentati contro le navi e altri di origine non del tutto chiara.

“Sommando le perdite documentate quotidianamente si ottiene un totale di circa ventimila chilometri quadrati, una superficie quasi equivalente a quella del Galles”, afferma Nina Noelle, esperta di disastri ambientali di Greenpeace.

Secondo Greenpeace, dall’inizio della guerra ci sono stati almeno 133 attacchi contro le petroliere. Ottobre è stato il mese peggiore, con più di trenta attacchi confermati o segnalati nello stretto di Hormuz e nelle acque circostanti, secondo il Washington institute for near east policy. Gli attacchi sono proseguiti anche a novembre.

Tra i più inquinanti di ottobre c’è quello contro la superpetroliera Gem No 2 al largo delle coste degli Emirati Arabi Uniti, che ha provocato una chiazza di petrolio lunga più di 35 chilometri. Un’immagine satellitare del 19 ottobre mostra un’enorme macchia nera nelle acque limpide al largo di Umm al Quwain.

Greenpeace stima che un attacco a una petroliera all’inizio di giugno abbia provocato una chiazza di più di seicento chilometri quadrati al largo delle coste dell’Oman. Due navi militari iraniane colpite a marzo hanno continuato a perdere petrolio per mesi, afferma Wim Zwijnenburg, ricercatore ambientale dell’organizzazione pacifista olandese Pax.

Anche un attacco alla Minoan Pioneer, una nave battente bandiera liberiana, avvenuto il 3 agosto, ha causato una grande chiazza di petrolio.

L’inquinamento da petrolio ha raggiunto varie coste dall’inizio della guerra. A marzo una chiazza proveniente dalla Shahid Bagheri è stata segnalata vicino alla foresta di mangrovie di Hara. Ad aprile l’inquinamento ha minacciato l’isola protetta di Shidvar, che ospita barriere coralline, uccelli marini e tartarughe. Ad agosto è stata segnalata la presenza di petrolio sulle rive dell’isola di Qeshm, vicino a importanti zone di pesca e siti di riproduzione delle tartarughe.

Le immagini satellitari mostrano inoltre chiazze di petrolio vicino al parco nazionale di Musandam, in Oman, e del delta del fiume Minab, in Iran, due aree ricche di fauna selvatica. Musandam ospita barriere coralline e siti di riproduzione di uccelli marini, mentre il delta del Minab ha piane di marea e foreste di mangrovie protette.

Le organizzazioni ambientaliste stanno continuando ad analizzare le immagini satellitari, ma avvertono che non è possibile valutare l’entità dei danni senza indagini sul campo, che rimangono estremamente difficili. Alcuni dei ricercatori e degli ambientalisti contattati in Iran e negli stati del Golfo hanno detto di aver ricevuto istruzioni dalle autorità di non parlare pubblicamente dei danni ambientali causati dalla guerra.

Stabilire le responsabilità non è facile, ma i Guardiani della rivoluzione, il corpo militare per la difesa del regime islamico dell’Iran, sono stati accusati della maggior parte degli attacchi. Anche le forze statunitensi hanno preso di mira le petroliere, mettendo fuori uso le navi iraniane che cercavano di aggirare il blocco navale e colpendone altre in risposta agli attacchi missilistici contro navi da guerra statunitensi.

Secondo un articolo del Wall Street Journal, il più grande sversamento di petrolio è stato però provocato da un attacco condotto dall’aeronautica militare degli Emirati Arabi Uniti contro i serbatoi di stoccaggio sull’isola iraniana di Lavan. Il greggio è finito nel Golfo, con ripercussioni sulle zone costiere, comprese le riserve naturali dell’isola di Shidvar.

Spiagge chiuse

In alcuni casi gli stati coinvolti hanno reagito prontamente alle perdite di petrolio. Dopo l’attacco alla Gem No 2, per esempio, gli Emirati Arabi Uniti hanno chiuso le spiagge, avviato un’operazione di bonifica e monitorato gli impianti di desalinizzazione. Il 30 ottobre le autorità hanno dichiarato che la perdita era stata tamponata e che l’inquinamento era in calo.

L’Oman ha inviato squadre di sommozzatori e attrezzature su una nave danneggiata per rimouovere il petrolio lungo più di dieci chilometri di costa vicino alle isole Hallaniyat.

Ma i danni ambientali più ampi potrebbero rivelarsi molto difficili da contenere. “Il petrolio potrebbe rimanere intrappolato nei sedimenti, sulle rive e nelle radici delle mangrovie per molto tempo dopo la scomparsa delle chiazze, danneggiando le catene alimentari marine e minacciando le comunità costiere che dipendono dalla pesca”, avverte Noelle.

La contaminazione può colpire organismi che vanno dai piccoli invertebrati ai pesci, agli uccelli e alle tartarughe. “Le mangrovie e le barriere coralline possono impiegare decenni per riprendersi, soprattutto se il petrolio rimane nei sedimenti”, aggiunge l’esperta di Greenpeace. “Le perdite ripetute, come quelle nello stretto di Hormuz, rischiano di aggravare le conseguenze ambientali”.

Depositi di catrame

Secondo Riegl, la guerra tra Iran e Iraq negli anni ottanta e la prima guerra del Golfo, tra il 1990 e il 1991, in cui furono prese di mira petroliere e giacimenti petroliferi, dimostrano le conseguenze durature dell’inquinamento sugli ecosistemi della regione.

Uno studio del 2020 ha attribuito alla guerra del Golfo i depositi di catrame ancora presenti sulle spiagge del Qatar. Da uno studio del 2022 è invece emerso che i sedimenti sull’isola di Abu Ali, in Arabia Saudita, sono ancora contaminati dagli sversamenti di petrolio di Nowruz del 1983-1985, quando durante la guerra tra Iran e Iraq finirono in mare circa 260mila tonnellate di greggio.

“Tutti gli animali che scavano nelle spiagge, tra cui le tartarughe marine quando depongono le uova, s’imbatteranno negli strati contaminati, con possibili conseguenze negative”, afferma Riegl. “Anche i granchi fantasma continueranno per anni a portare in superficie materiale contaminato”.

“Ovviamente gli effetti dell’inquinamento da petrolio saranno ancora rilevabili tra decenni, quindi si tratta di un problema generazionale”, conclude il biologo. “Rischiamo davvero di perdere qualcosa d’insostituibile”. ◆

articles.title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
articles.summary: Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

articles.body:
Kosovo: New Thaci conviction reignites debate about justice

November 17, 2026

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Swift response from government

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

Government set up working group

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

Parliament considers amending law

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

'Room for criticism of both sides'

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
articles.summary: Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?
articles.preview: Saudi Arabia: Crackdown on dissent intensifies amid Iran war November 17, 2026 Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression? Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia: Crackdown on dissent intensifies amid Iran war

November 17, 2026

Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?

Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM, the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Leah Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.

This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST, echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.

DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

articles.title: Microsoft, un 'bug' nascosto da luglio ha causato il grande disservizio
articles.summary: "Problema tecnico non correlato ad attacchi informatici o ad attività di IA"
articles.preview: Un difetto nascosto da luglio è stato la causa di uno dei più vasti disservizi nella storia di Microsoft verificatosi la scorsa settimana. Lo afferma la stessa società di Redmond che, dopo le ipotesi degli esperti, ha pubblicato un rapporto ufficiale sull'incidente spiegando come questo bug latente, insieme a variazioni nel traffico e a una ridotta capacità dei server, abbia provocato la tempesta perfetta per il blocco dell'intera infrastruttura Microsoft 365 ed Exchange.
articles.body:
Un difetto nascosto da luglio è stato la causa di uno dei più vasti disservizi nella storia di Microsoft verificatosi la scorsa settimana. Lo afferma la stessa società di Redmond che, dopo le ipotesi degli esperti, ha pubblicato un rapporto ufficiale sull'incidente spiegando come questo bug latente, insieme a variazioni nel traffico e a una ridotta capacità dei server, abbia provocato la tempesta perfetta per il blocco dell'intera infrastruttura Microsoft 365 ed Exchange.

Nel documento, la società definisce l'accaduto come "un problema tecnico non correlato ad attacchi informatici o ad attività di intelligenza artificiale/agenti". L'interruzione si è verificata esattamente tra le 17:20 ora italiana del 12 novembre e le 17:10 del 13 novembre, quasi 24 ore. Il monitoraggio è proseguito fino al 14 novembre.

Il disservizio viene dunque attribuito a tre fattori. Una modifica apportata al gateway cloud di Microsoft (permette ai servizi di accedere, interrogare o aggiornare dati che si trovano all'interno della rete dell'azienda) a partire da luglio che ha generato un bug per cui in determinate condizioni le risorse di memoria potevano esaurirsi rendendo il sistema non più reattivo. Secondo Microsoft, il difetto non è mai emerso durante i test preliminari poiché l'hardware utilizzato era meno potente, mentre l'uso di macchine più recenti ha contribuito al blocco. Il secondo fattore ha riguardato il carico sui server dovuto a "spostamenti di traffico durante normali operazioni di manutenzione e aggiornamento della rete" relativi a Teams. Si è così innescato un effetto a valanga, che ha portato al blocco di oltre l'80% dei server gateway Microsoft coinvolti.

Una volta tornati online, spiega il colosso tecnologico, i server si sono trovati di fronte a lunghe code di richieste in attesa di accesso, il che ha immediatamente innescato lo stesso esaurimento delle risorse che aveva causato l'interruzione iniziale. E dato che il bug risalente a luglio non era ancora stato individuato, anche il ripristino del sistema a uno stato precedente si è rivelato inefficace. I server sono stati aggiornati e rimessi in funzione gradualmente.

Microsoft prevede di pubblicare il rapporto finale sull'incidente il 20 novembre. Il documento potrebbe fornire chiarimenti sui motivi per cui i sistemi di isolamento regionale non hanno funzionato e sulle misure correttive che verranno adottate per scongiurare il ripetersi di gravi interruzioni.

articles.title: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
articles.summary: The firm started just five years ago and is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.
articles.preview: Anthropic is poised to hit a value of up to $1.5tn (£1.14tn) when its shares start trading on the stock market on Thursday. The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York. That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.
articles.body:
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of up to $1.5tn (£1.14tn) when its shares start trading on the stock market on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.

It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable.

The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.

The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.

If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Crucial test for AI

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.

However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price.

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.

The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.

Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.

- The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

- Published3 hours ago

There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.

"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.

Rapid rise

Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.

The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.

It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.

CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.

The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.

Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.

Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.

Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.

A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

articles.title: Anthropic IPO raises $107.3 billion to top SpaceX’s record debut
articles.summary: The artificial intelligence firm priced its shares at $83 each, above a range of $70 to $78 marketed in its filing.
articles.preview: Anthropic and its seven co-founders have raised $107.3 billion in an upsized initial public offering and private placement, becoming the first frontier artificial intelligence lab tapping the public markets to fund its development of thinking machines. The AI firm sold 956.4 million shares and the co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for $83 each, according to a statement Wednesday confirming an earlier report, above the marketed range.
articles.body:
Anthropic and its seven co-founders have raised $107.3 billion in an upsized initial public offering and private placement, becoming the first frontier artificial intelligence lab tapping the public markets to fund its development of thinking machines.

The AI firm sold 956.4 million shares and the co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for $83 each, according to a statement Wednesday confirming an earlier report, above the marketed range. The company had marketed 801.4 million shares, while the co-founders offered 23.6 million shares, in a range of $70 to $78 each, according to its filings.

The offering also includes a $26 billion private placement listed in Anthropic’s filings, with firms including Alphabet’s Google, Advanced Micro Devices and Microsoft participating. Anthropic’s IPO is the biggest of all time even without the placement, with the $81.3 billion base deal topping SpaceX’s $75 billion.

articles.title: Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all time
articles.summary: AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.
articles.preview: AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut. Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June. The San Francisco-based AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each. The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts.
articles.body:
AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.

Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June.

The San Francisco-based AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.

The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts.

Anthropic had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece.

The Claude creator is also set to raise $26bn through a private placement, a type of deal involving the sale of stock private investors, taking the total capital raised to $107.3bn.

SpaceX’s total IPO haul came to $85.7bn, after the deal’s underwriters exercised an overallotment option to purchase additional shares

The blockbuster offering gives Anthropic a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, making it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla.

‘ANT’

Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.

The public listing of Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers from rival AI firm OpenAI, has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the AI rollout.

Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI, expecting it to usher in revolutionary changes in business and society.

AI-related spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

Companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the S&P 500 index.

The spending frenzy has stoked debate over whether Big Tech is funding a future gold mine or a speculative bubble like the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.

Nvidia woes

Anthropic’s listing also comes as the market for the advanced GPUs that power AI is under a cloud amid the spying claims roiling chip giant Nvidia.

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week amid unproven claims that a woman he was romantically involved with worked with the Chinese intelligence services.

The scandal has fueled calls in the US for stronger restrictions on China’s access to high-end chips, casting a pall over an AI boom partly sustained by Chinese developers’ remote access to data centres in Southeast Asia.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index has shed nearly 7.6 percent of its value over the best month, led by a more than 30 percent plunge in Nvidia’s stock price.

Asian stock markets with heavy exposure to AI fell on Thursday despite the flurry of excitement around Anthropic, with South Korea’s Kospi, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index and Taiwan’s Taiex all in the red in morning trading.

Investor confidence in AI

Jay R Ritter, an IPO expert at the University of Florida, said that Anthropic’s ability to make profits to justify its valuation will depend on various factors, some of which are outside of its control.

“Thirty years ago, the internet was the next big thing. It has changed our lives,” Ritter told Al Jazeera. “Today, artificial intelligence is the next big thing. It will change our lives, too.”

Ritter said investors are particularly excited about the potential of Anthropic’s AI models to find cures to conditions such as cancer and dementia in the near future.

“When Google went public in 2004, no one knew whether it would be able to dominate on-line searches, and no one knew how lucrative the targeted search advertising business would become,” he said.

Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Anthropic’s strong debut should help reassure investors that the AI boom is sustainble.

“At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Ives said in a note to clients

“It is going through a very turbulent, white-knuckle period that does not change our longer-term view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion of capex will be spent over the next few years on the AI revolution, and this sets the stage for the next phase of tech and infrastructure investment with Anthropic a central player in the buildout,” Ives said.

articles.title: Anthropic fissa il prezzo a 83 dollari, verso l'Ipo più grande della storia
articles.summary: Batte SpaceX di Elon Musk. Il boom di richieste porta la capitalizzazione a 1.500 miliardi
articles.preview: Anthropic fissa il prezzo della sua offerta pubblica iniziale a 83 dollari per azione, più dell'intervallo di 70-78 dollari atteso, secondo il Wall Street Journal, in base al boom delle domanda di sottoscrizione: 400 miliardi da parte degli investitori istituzionali e di 100 miliardi nella componente retail. La società guidata da Dario Amodei getta così le basi per l'Ipo più grande della storia, la prima di un importante sviluppatore di modelli IA di frontiera.
articles.body:
Anthropic fissa il prezzo della sua offerta pubblica iniziale a 83 dollari per azione, più dell'intervallo di 70-78 dollari atteso, secondo il Wall Street Journal, in base al boom delle domanda di sottoscrizione: 400 miliardi da parte degli investitori istituzionali e di 100 miliardi nella componente retail. La società guidata da Dario Amodei getta così le basi per l'Ipo più grande della storia, la prima di un importante sviluppatore di modelli IA di frontiera.

L'operazione consentirebbe la raccolta di almeno 68 miliardi, a cui aggiungere altri 26 miliardi generati da un collocamento privato da parte di colossi legati all'IA, a partire dai produttori di microchip: Amd, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia e Tmsc. Il totale di oltre 94 miliardi, nei calcoli di Bloomberg, supererebbe gli 86,2 miliardi dell'Ipo di SpaceX, voluta da Elon Musk a giugno. La valutazione di Anthropic, fondata poco più di cinque anni fa, si attesterebbe intorno ai 1.500 miliardi.

Anthropic, che esordirà domani al Nasdaq con il ticker 'Ant', è un test sul settore dell'IA, dopo lo scandalo Nvidia e la caduta del carismatico ceo Jensen Huang. La tanto attesa quotazione ha risentito di molte pressioni, ma ha mantenuto tutte le caratteristiche di benchmark come prima compagnia dell'IA a sfidare i mercati: la valutazione della startup è scesa dagli oltre 2.000 miliardi di dollari di inizio anno.

Ora, l'ideatore della famiglia di modelli di grandi dimensioni e di assistenti basati su IA, noti come Claude, sarà domani su mercati già turbolenti, scossi dai dubbi sul finanziamento della rivoluzione dell'intelligenza artificiale, alla base del ritardo dell'Ipo di altre società. Le elezioni Usa di midterm hanno dato la scossa facendo emergere l'avversione verso i data center su scala nazionale, ma necessari per le capacità di calcolo, mentre l'uscita della scorsa settimana di Huang da Nvidia, tra i più ferventi sostenitori dell'IA con la gamma di microchip dedicati, ha aggiunto altra incertezza, nel mezzo di indagini del board e del governo Usa sui suoi legami con una presunta spia cinese e su possibili spedizioni al Dragone di chip proibiti.

Nvidia, intanto, ha interrotto l'export di spedizioni verso la Cina dei chip IA della serie 'Hopper', progettata per accelerare l'addestramento di modelli: nel gruppo c'è il potente H200, la cui vendita a Pechino era stata approvata dal Dipartimento del Commercio Usa lo scorso gennaio. Una prossima stretta potrebbe colpire la 'distillazione', il metodo di addestramento dell'IA in cui un modello più piccolo e meno potente viene creato usando gli output di un modello preesistente e più avanzato. I player cinesi sono sospettati di abusarne a danno dei colossi Usa, secondo il segretario al Tesoro, Scott Bessent.

L'Ipo di Anthropic fornirà agli investitori un prezzo di mercato per valutare la crescita di ricavi e costi di calcolo di un laboratorio Ia. Dai documenti depositati, i ricavi della startup sono passati dai 386 milioni del 2024 ai 4,6 miliardi del 2025, per poi raggiungere i 33,2 miliardi nei primi 9 mesi del 2026 (di cui 17 miliardi solo nel terzo trimestre). Oltre il 70% dei ricavi deriva da commissioni sul consumo: i clienti pagano per la potenza di calcolo usata, con una tariffa calcolata in base ai token, l'unità dati fondamentale letta e scritta dai modelli Claude. La parte residua fa capo agli abbonamenti a Claude. A dispetto della crescita enorme dei ricavi, Anthropic non ha ancora raggiunto la redditività: pesano gli investimenti ingenti per i costi di calcolo, la voce di spesa principale. Nel 2026, Anthropic ha avuto una perdita netta di 104 miliardi a fine settembre, con spese di calcolo e infrastrutture per 18,8 miliardi nei primi nove mesi, salite dai 4,4 miliardi dell'anno precedente.

Sam Altman, a capo della rivale OpenAI, ha assicurato che la sua società "sarà quotata in Borsa, prima o poi", con l'ambizione di bilanciare prima "redditività e sicurezza": la sua Ipo è scivolata al 2027.

articles.body:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

articles.body:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies.

“It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report.

While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft.

“I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”

Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO.

“Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.”

articles.body:
Anthropic has reportedly priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO.

Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers. Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Spark Ventures, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company.

Some of the company’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they were reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO.

Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the Claude maker’s strategic partners, Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

The company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.

articles.title: Nvidia created a weird bit of intrigue by not filing a routine SEC report
articles.summary: One Wall Street analyst got to the bottom of Nvidia's surprise announcement that it wouldn't be filing its formal quarterly results document, the 10-Q, for weeks.
articles.preview: During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why. The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.
articles.body:
During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.

The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.

The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.

The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.

“The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).

Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.

So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.)

The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.

Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.

There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”

articles.title: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
articles.summary: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.
articles.preview: It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice. Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world. articles.body:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival â Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

A benchmark valuation

At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."

What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.

It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."

So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.

But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.

It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.

Public doubts

It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.

If Anthropic â and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.

Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.

He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

Hype and FOMO

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it â the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development â means that buying interest is high.

It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.

With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.

Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.

The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.

Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.

"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

articles.body:
If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.

It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.

Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?

But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.

On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.

“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”

Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.

In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.

Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

articles.title: British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
articles.summary: Tyler Buchanan, from Dundee, was a member of the notorious Scattered Spider group and began hacking when he was a teenager.
articles.preview: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims. Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.
articles.body:
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.

Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.

Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.

Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.

The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.

The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".

The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.

The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.

In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

Threatened with a blowtorch

Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.

In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.

Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.

Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.

In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.

Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.

The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.

He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.

After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.

They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.

Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is seeking information from US artificial intelligence firm Anthropic over the alleged use of its technology in a political influence operation targeting Malaysian voters, the government has said. Anthropic said in a report issued in September it had uncovered a suspected AI-powered campaign meant to disrupt elections in the Southeast Asian nation.
articles.body:
US artificial intelligence firm Anthropic said in September it had uncovered a suspected AI-powered campaign meant to disrupt elections in Malaysia.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is seeking information from US artificial intelligence firm Anthropic over the alleged use of its technology in a political influence operation targeting Malaysian voters, the government has said.

Anthropic said in a report issued in September it had uncovered a suspected AI-powered campaign meant to disrupt elections in the Southeast Asian nation.

It pointed to an "overseas entity", believed to have been based in Turkey, that abused Anthropic's Claude AI model to generate around 1,000 fake accounts on social media platform X and create a synthetic news site.

"Based on the report, Anthropic alleged that Claude technology was used by an overseas entity to develop several components of the operation, including a targeting system, a network of fake social media accounts, fake news sites and related components," the Malaysian communications ministry told parliament in a written statement on Tuesday (Nov 17), responding to a lawmaker's questions about the matter.

The ministry said the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission was "seeking further information and clarification from Anthropic regarding the report", and would then "determine appropriate follow-up actions".

According to Anthropic's report, the entity "sold access to the platform as a paid influence-as-a-service capability", marketing the infrastructure as "military-grade, AI-driven, real-time political operations ecosystem".

"The operation involved the actors leveraging that platform built through Claude to profile and target voters in Malaysia, constituency by constituency, using census and electoral data that they had ingested," the report said.

But the campaign was stopped "without evidence of breakout into authentic communities", it said.

The report did not specify when the operation began or how long it lasted, but detailed Anthropic's efforts to disrupt misuse of its AI models between December 2025 and August 2026.

The communications ministry said Malaysia was drafting a bill to "strengthen the country's AI governance framework".

"The government will continue to strengthen monitoring of the risks of misuse of AI technology as well as collaboration with technology providers, digital platforms and relevant agencies to address online harm and ensure that the country's digital environment remains safe, transparent and trusted," it said.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa kicked off a week-long artificial intelligence mission in California on Monday, seeking to draw investment from US tech giants against a backdrop of strained political ties with Washington.

He addressed a gathering of tech founders, investors, and global policymakers to discuss the future of the technology sector.

Through this California tour, Pretoria aims to establish South Africa as a premier hub for digital innovation on the African continent and secure foreign capital to modernize its economy.

Ramaphosa's itinerary includes high-level meetings with executives from Google, Microsoft, and Cisco, as well as a stop at Stanford University.
